title: AQA GCSE English Language Paper 2: Questions, Marks and Revision Strategy
description: A practical guide to AQA GCSE English Language Paper 2, covering the 4, 8, 12 and 16-mark reading questions plus the 40-mark viewpoint-writing task.

children: AQA GCSE English Language Paper 2 tests how well you can understand and compare viewpoints across two non-fiction texts, then communicate your own viewpoint in writing. The paper lasts 1 hour 45 minutes and is worth 80 marks: 40 for reading and 40 for writing. This guide gives a practical revision strategy for each part of the paper.
AQA English Language Paper 2 at a Glance
Section A uses two linked non-fiction texts from different time periods. Section B asks you to write your own viewpoint for a specified audience, purpose and form.
Question 1 – 4 marks
A short AO1 question. Read the wording carefully and select the required information from the specified source. Precision matters more than explanation.
Question 2 – 8 marks
A summary question assessing AO1 across both sources. You need to infer and synthesise differences or similarities, using relevant details from each text.

Question 3 is worth 12 marks and focuses on language analysis in one source. Question 4 is worth 16 marks and compares writers’ viewpoints and how they are conveyed. Question 5 is worth 40 marks and assesses viewpoint writing, split into 24 marks for content and organisation and 16 for technical accuracy.
Revision priority:
Do not revise Paper 2 as one large skill. Practise each question separately first, then combine them in timed sections and finally complete full papers.

Question 1 and Question 2: Retrieval, Inference and Summary
The first two questions reward accurate reading rather than feature spotting. Your job is to select the right evidence and make concise, relevant inferences.
For Question 1
work only from the source and lines named in the question. Avoid explaining answers that only need selecting or identifying.
For Question 2
build each paragraph around a clear difference or similarity. Use evidence from both sources and explain what each detail shows before linking them together.
Common mistake
Students often copy quotations without stating the inference. The mark comes from showing what the evidence tells you, not from simply finding a matching phrase.

Question 3: Language Analysis – 12 Marks

Question 3 asks you to analyse how a writer uses language to achieve effects. Strong answers focus closely on words and phrases, then explain what those choices suggest and why they are effective in context.
Start with the wording
Choose a precise word or short phrase that gives you something worthwhile to analyse. Long quotations usually make the analysis less focused.
Explain meaning before terminology
A named technique is useful only when it helps explain the writer’s choice. Do not treat device spotting as the analysis itself.
Develop the effect
Explore connotations, tone, imagery or associations and link them back to the question. Aim to say more than ‘this makes the reader want to read on’.
Use several developed examples
A small number of well-analysed quotations is usually more effective than a long list of techniques with one sentence on each.
Be accurate
Technical vocabulary should clarify your analysis, not replace it. If you are unsure of a label, explain the language precisely instead of forcing a term.
Practice method:

Take one paragraph from a source, choose three short quotations and write one developed explanation for each. Then compare your response with the assessment objective and improve the weakest explanation.
Question 4: Comparing Viewpoints – 16 Marks
Question 4 is the major comparison question. You need to compare the writers’ perspectives and analyse how each writer communicates those viewpoints.
Compare ideas directly
Make the relationship between the writers explicit: similarly, whereas, however, both writers, in contrast. Do not write two separate mini-essays and leave the comparison until the end.
Compare methods as well as viewpoints
Use evidence from both sources and analyse how language, tone, emphasis, examples or other choices help each writer present a perspective.
Stay focused on the question
The best evidence is not necessarily the most dramatic quotation. Select details that reveal the writers’ attitudes towards the specific issue named in the task.
Develop the comparison
Move beyond ‘Writer A is positive and Writer B is negative’. Explain the precise nature of each viewpoint and how strongly, cautiously, critically or enthusiastically it is expressed.
Useful paragraph shape:

State the comparison, support Writer A with a short quotation and analysis, then connect Writer B directly to that idea with its own evidence and analysis before explaining the significance of the contrast or similarity.
Question 5: Writing to Present a Viewpoint – 40 Marks
Question 5 asks you to communicate a clear viewpoint for a specified audience, purpose and form. It is worth half the paper, so it needs deliberate planning and enough time for a developed response.
24 marks: content and organisation
Develop a convincing viewpoint, shape ideas deliberately, use paragraphs purposefully and adapt tone and structure to the audience and form.
16 marks: technical accuracy
Control spelling, punctuation and grammar, and use a range of sentence structures accurately. Variety only helps when it is controlled.
Plan the argument
Choose your central viewpoint and three or four developed lines of argument. Decide how the opening establishes your position and how the ending leaves a clear final impression.
Use rhetoric selectively
Questions, repetition, contrast, anecdote and direct address can be effective, but they should serve the argument. A checklist of persuasive devices is not a substitute for coherent reasoning.
Proofread strategically
Leave time to check sentence boundaries, apostrophes, commonly misspelt words and places where punctuation has become over-ambitious or unclear.

A sensible revision sequence is: master each question type without time pressure, practise short timed responses, complete timed sections, then sit full papers. After every attempt, identify one recurring weakness and make that the focus of the next practice session.

Paper 2 becomes much more manageable when you treat it as five specific tasks rather than one general English exam. Know what each question is assessing, select evidence carefully, explain rather than label, compare directly and give Question 5 the planning and checking time its 40 marks justify.
